papers.title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety lies at the core of developing and deploying large language models (LLMs). However, previous safety benchmarks only concern the safety in one language, e.g. the majority language in the pretraining data such as English. In this work, we build the first multilingual safety benchmark for LLMs, XSafety, in response to the global deployment of LLMs in practice. XSafety covers 14 kinds of commonly used safety issues across 10 languages that span several language families. We utilize XSafety to empirically study the multilingual safety for 4 widely-used LLMs, including both close-API and open-source models. Experimental results show that all LLMs produce significantly more unsafe responses for non-English queries than English ones, indicating the necessity of developing safety alignment for non-English languages. In addition, we propose several simple and effective prompting methods to improve the multilingual safety of ChatGPT by evoking safety knowledge and improving cross-lingual generalization of safety alignment. Our prompting method can significantly reduce the ratio of unsafe responses from 19.1% to 9.7% for non-English queries. We release our data at https://github.com/Jarviswang94/Multilingual_safety_benchmark.

papers.title: Safety Assessment of Chinese Large Language Models
papers.abstract: With the rapid popularity of large language models such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, a growing amount of attention is paid to their safety concerns. These models may generate insulting and discriminatory content, reflect incorrect social values, and may be used for malicious purposes such as fraud and dissemination of misleading information. Evaluating and enhancing their safety is particularly essential for the wide application of large language models (LLMs). To further promote the safe deployment of LLMs, we develop a Chinese LLM safety assessment benchmark. Our benchmark explores the comprehensive safety performance of LLMs from two perspectives: 8 kinds of typical safety scenarios and 6 types of more challenging instruction attacks. Our benchmark is based on a straightforward process in which it provides the test prompts and evaluates the safety of the generated responses from the evaluated model. In evaluation, we utilize the LLM's strong evaluation ability and develop it as a safety evaluator by prompting. On top of this benchmark, we conduct safety assessments and analyze 15 LLMs including the OpenAI GPT series and other well-known Chinese LLMs, where we observe some interesting findings. For example, we find that instruction attacks are more likely to expose safety issues of all LLMs. Moreover, to promote the development and deployment of safe, responsible, and ethical AI, we publicly release SafetyPrompts including 100k augmented prompts and responses by LLMs.

papers.title: Safety at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey of Large Model and Agent Safety
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large models, driven by their exceptional abilities in learning and generalization through large-scale pre-training, has reshaped the landscape of Artificial Intelligence (AI). These models are now foundational to a wide range of applications, including conversational AI, recommendation systems, autonomous driving, content generation, medical diagnostics, and scientific discovery. However, their widespread deployment also exposes them to significant safety risks, raising concerns about robustness, reliability, and ethical implications. This survey provides a systematic review of current safety research on large models, covering Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Diffusion Models (DMs), and large-model-powered Agents. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We present a comprehensive taxonomy of safety threats to these models, including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, backdoor attacks, jailbreak and prompt injection attacks, energy-latency attacks, data and model extraction attacks, and emerging agent-specific threats. (2) We review defense strategies proposed for each type of attacks if available and summarize the commonly used datasets and benchmarks for safety research. (3) Building on this, we identify and discuss the open challenges in large model safety, emphasizing the need for comprehensive safety evaluations, scalable and effective defense mechanisms, and sustainable data practices. More importantly, we highlight the necessity of collective efforts from the research community and international collaboration. Our work can serve as a useful reference for researchers and practitioners, fostering the ongoing development of comprehensive defense systems and platforms to safeguard AI models.

papers.title: Enhanced Diagnostic and Interpretable Model for Febrile Diseases Using Explainable AI and Large Language Model
papers.abstract: <p><span>Tropical febrile diseases pose significant public health challenges in tropical regions, particularly in resource-limited settings, where timely and accurate diagnoses are critical for effective disease management. However, existing diagnostic systems are black-box and often lack interpretability, making it difficult for healthcare practitioners to understand and trust machine learning (ML) predictions. Additionally, the existing system excludes younger patients, limiting its applicability. This study aimed to develop an integrated diagnostic system that enhances interpretability by leveraging machine learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), and a large language model (LLM). A dataset comprising 3,914 patient records with 32 symptoms was obtained from a New Frontiers in Research Fund-sponsored project and preprocessed for analysis. Random Forest (RF) was trained with hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation to optimize its performance. The tuned model achieved high diagnostic performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in diagnosing six febrile diseases. To enhance interpretability, a Model Interpretability Framework (MIF) was incorporated, integrating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) for visual insights and ChatGPT for textual explanations. This combination provided users with a clear understanding of the diagnostic process, addressing the limitations of black-box ML models. The system was implemented using Python in a development environment that included Google Colaboratory, Visual Studio Code, Flet, and MySQL for database management. Agile development methodology and Unified Modeling Language tools were employed to create a user-friendly design for clinicians and patients. The diagnostic system was evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics. The RF model achieved outstanding precision for most diseases, high recall (≥0.97), and an AUC-ROC of 0.99, indicating nearly flawless training performance with few misclassifications. On the test dataset, the model performed better in diagnosing malaria (F1-score = 88%, precision = 85%), urinary tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 80%), and respiratory tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 77%). The evaluated system demonstrated strong predictive performance, correctly identifying 72 out of 99 tested patient cases, with 26 cases misclassified and one case completely missed. It achieved the highest detection rates for Malaria and HIV/AIDS, accurately identifying all cases without false positives. This work enhances diagnostic solutions for tropical healthcare settings by improving explainability and ensuring inclusivity for younger patients, addressing key limitations in existing systems. The integration of ML, XAI, and LLM enhances diagnostic performance and lays the groundwork for future AI-driven healthcare innovations, ultimately improving health outcomes in resource-scarce regions. Healthcare providers should adopt this system to enhance the efficiency of disease diagnosis and extend the system to diagnose additional medical conditions.&nbsp;</span></p>

summary: The retrieved literature highlights significant safety concerns in large language models (LLMs), particularly in multilingual contexts, and proposes benchmarks for assessing their safety across various languages. It identifies gaps in the generalizability of findings and the need for comprehensive safety evaluations, especially for non-English models. Additionally, the integration of LLMs in few-shot recommender systems shows potential for enhancing performance, though empirical validation remains limited. Overall, the studies emphasize the importance of interpretability and safety in AI applications, particularly in healthcare diagnostics.
scholarly_positioning: Existing research has primarily focused on safety assessments of large language models (LLMs) within specific linguistic and contextual frameworks, revealing significant gaps in multilingual safety and the generalizability of findings. While benchmarks like XSafety address safety concerns, they often lack comprehensive empirical validation and fail to explore the long-term effectiveness of proposed enhancements across diverse applications. Furthermore, the integration of LLMs in few-shot recommender systems has shown promise but lacks detailed methodologies and empirical results to substantiate claims. This proposed research aims to bridge these gaps by developing interpretable internal representations that enhance both safety and controllability in LLMs, contributing to a broader discourse on the necessity for robust, interpretable AI systems in critical applications such as healthcare.

research_scope: This study will evaluate the safety and interpretability of large language models (LLMs) specifically in the context of healthcare diagnostics for febrile diseases. The target population will include three Chinese LLMs, and the technical task will involve assessing their performance in generating safe and interpretable diagnostic outputs. The evaluation period will span six months, during which the models will be benchmarked against a multilingual safety assessment framework. A control group will consist of traditional diagnostic systems without LLM integration. Primary outcomes will include the frequency of unsafe responses and the interpretability of diagnostic recommendations, while secondary outcomes will assess user trust and satisfaction through human evaluations.

{

  "Internal Representations": "The encoded information within the model that reflects its understanding and processing of input data, crucial for interpretability.",
  "Interpretability Method": "Techniques used to explain model decisions, including probing (analyzing model layers), attribution (assigning importance to inputs), attention visualization (showing focus areas), and explanation generation (creating human-readable justifications).",
  "Explanation Audience": "The intended recipients of model explanations, which in this context include researchers (for model understanding), system developers (for integration), and end-users (for trust and usability).",
  "Safety Outcomes": "Metrics to evaluate the safety of model outputs, including unsafe response rate (frequency of harmful outputs), over-refusal (excessive avoidance of providing answers), jailbreak success (ability to bypass safety measures), harmful compliance (following harmful instructions), and refusal precision/recall (accuracy of safe refusals).",
  "User Trust": "The degree of confidence users have in the model's outputs, assessed through trust calibration (alignment of perceived vs. actual trust), blind trust (unquestioning reliance), perceived transparency (clarity of model operations), and appropriate reliance (using model outputs judiciously).",
  "Safety and Controllability": "The ability to ensure that LLM outputs are safe and manageable, minimizing risks while maximizing user control over model interactions.",
  "Alignment": "The degree to which model outputs are consistent with human values and intentions, particularly important in sensitive applications like healthcare.",
  "Fairness": "Ensuring that model outputs do not discriminate against any group, maintaining equitable treatment across diverse populations."

question: How do interpretable internal representations of three Chinese large language models affect the safety and interpretability of diagnostic outputs in healthcare for febrile diseases compared to traditional diagnostic systems?
theoretical_mechanism: The independent variable is the interpretable internal representations of the three Chinese large language models (LLMs). These representations serve as a mediator by influencing the system-level outcomes, such as unsafe response rate and refusal accuracy, through technical mechanisms like safety detection and steering filters. The dependent variables include system-level outcomes (e.g., jailbreak success, controllability) and user-level outcomes (e.g., trust, satisfaction). The theoretical framework is based on the interaction between model interpretability and user perception, where enhanced interpretability leads to improved safety outcomes, which in turn fosters user trust and satisfaction. The causal chain posits that better internal representations enhance safety mechanisms, reducing unsafe outputs, which positively impacts user trust and satisfaction. Assumptions requiring empirical validation include the effectiveness of interpretability techniques in improving safety outcomes and the direct influence of user trust on the adoption of model outputs.
hypothesis: Interpretable internal representations of three Chinese large language models will significantly reduce the unsafe response rate compared to traditional diagnostic systems, with enhanced interpretability mediating this relationship, leading to increased user trust in the diagnostic outputs.

proposal: This research proposal aims to investigate the impact of interpretable internal representations in three Chinese large language models (LLMs) on the safety and controllability of diagnostic outputs in healthcare for febrile diseases. Key concepts include 'Large Language Models' as AI systems generating human-like text, 'Internal Representations' as the encoded information reflecting model understanding, and 'Safety Outcomes' as metrics evaluating harmful outputs. The study assumes access to open-source LLMs, labeled datasets, and human participants for trust evaluations. Motivated by significant safety concerns in healthcare diagnostics, the proposal positions itself within the domain of LLM safety and human-computer interaction, addressing a critical gap in the literature regarding the long-term effectiveness of safety enhancements across multilingual contexts. The central research question is: How do interpretable internal representations of three Chinese LLMs affect the safety and interpretability of diagnostic outputs compared to traditional systems? The theoretical mechanism posits that enhanced interpretability (independent variable) mediates improved safety outcomes (system-level) such as reduced unsafe response rates, which in turn fosters increased user trust and satisfaction (user-level). The falsifiable hypothesis states that interpretable internal representations will significantly reduce unsafe responses compared to traditional systems, with enhanced interpretability mediating this relationship. Constructs will be operationalized using metrics like unsafe response rate and user trust, measured through response classification metrics and trust calibration surveys. The methodology will employ benchmark evaluations against traditional diagnostic systems, ensuring robust comparisons of safety outcomes, with controls for confounding variables such as user familiarity with AI systems. Expected contributions include a novel theoretical framework linking interpretability to user trust, a multilingual safety assessment framework, and empirical evidence on the effectiveness of interpretable representations. Key limitations include potential biases in training data and the inability to generalize findings beyond the specific context of Chinese LLMs in healthcare diagnostics, alongside risks of unsafe response generation and interpretability issues, which will be mitigated through rigorous safety filtering and the use of multiple interpretability techniques.

Enhance the operationalization section by ensuring all constructs have clear measurement instruments and addressing confounding variables in detail. Finally, improve the clarity of contributions by structuring them more explicitly and emphasizing their novelty.

rubric_scores.level: 12-13: strong and clear research framing with minor conceptual weaknesses
rubric_scores.justification: The proposal articulates a clear research problem regarding the safety and interpretability of LLMs in healthcare diagnostics. However, while key concepts are defined, some operational definitions could be more precise, particularly regarding how 'safety outcomes' are measured. Major weaknesses: Vague definitions of key constructs such as 'safety outcomes' and 'interpretability' could lead to ambiguity in measurement and evaluation. Next band requirements: To move into the next band, the proposal needs to provide more precise operational definitions and clarify the boundaries of the research problem.

rubric_scores.level: 9-11: generally connected but some weak transitions or unsupported assumptions
rubric_scores.justification: The proposal presents a logical flow from problem identification to hypothesis formulation. However, some assumptions regarding the effectiveness of interpretability techniques are not sufficiently justified. Major weaknesses: Weak transitions between the theoretical mechanism and the proposed methodology, particularly in justifying how internal representations will directly influence safety outcomes. Next band requirements: Strengthening the justification for causal claims and ensuring that each component logically connects to the next would improve coherence.

rubric_scores.level: 15-17: clear novelty with meaningful research differentiation
rubric_scores.justification: The proposal introduces a novel theoretical framework linking interpretability to user trust and safety outcomes, which is a meaningful contribution to the field of LLM safety. Major weaknesses: While the theoretical contribution is strong, the empirical aspects could benefit from more innovative methodologies rather than relying on existing frameworks. Next band requirements: To achieve a higher score, the proposal should demonstrate more methodological innovation in evaluating the proposed constructs.

The methodology outlines a benchmark evaluation approach, but lacks detailed plans for addressing potential confounding variables and ensuring reproducibility. Major weaknesses: Insufficient detail on how to control for confounding variables and the lack of a clear plan for participant recruitment and ethics approval. Next band requirements: Providing a more detailed experimental design that includes controls for confounding variables and a clear recruitment strategy would enhance feasibility.

rubric_scores.level: 12-13: strong literature grounding with good comparative analysis
rubric_scores.justification: The proposal effectively situates itself within existing literature, identifying gaps in multilingual safety assessments and interpretability in healthcare diagnostics. Major weaknesses: While the literature review is solid, it could benefit from a more critical analysis of competing approaches and a deeper exploration of unresolved tensions in the field. Next band requirements: To improve, the proposal should engage more critically with existing literature and articulate how the proposed research addresses specific gaps.

rubric_scores.level: 7-8: approaching PhD-level with some shallow areas
rubric_scores.justification: The proposal demonstrates a reasonable level of theoretical sophistication but lacks depth in discussing the mechanisms behind the proposed relationships. Major weaknesses: Limited discussion on the broader implications of the research and the mechanisms that explain why interpretability should enhance safety outcomes. Next band requirements: Incorporating a more detailed discussion of theoretical mechanisms and broader implications would strengthen the academic depth.

The proposal is generally well-structured and clear, with appropriate academic tone and terminology. Major weaknesses: Some sections could be more concise, and minor grammatical issues detract from overall clarity. Next band requirements: Improving conciseness and addressing grammatical issues would enhance the overall presentation.

evaluation.comments: Total score: 75.0/100. Academic level: Master's-level. Major strengths: Clear identification of a significant research problem.; Strong theoretical contribution linking interpretability to user trust.; Good engagement with existing literature. Major weaknesses: Vague operational definitions of key constructs.; Insufficient justification for causal claims.; Lack of methodological innovation and detail. Required improvements for true PhD-level quality: Provide precise operational definitions for key constructs.; Strengthen causal reasoning and justification for assumptions.; Enhance methodological rigor and detail in experimental design. Final verdict: The proposal demonstrates potential but lacks the depth and rigor expected of PhD-level research, requiring significant improvements in clarity, methodology, and theoretical grounding.
